paragraphs: Tesco is a big supermarket company. Its Irish business made more money last year.
Its profit before tax went up by about 9%. It was €211.6 million. Total sales were €3.75 billion.
Tesco Ireland sent €120 million to its owner in Britain. It also paid about €32 million in tax.
The company opened nine new shops. Its online shopping grew fast. Tesco now has 194 shops in Ireland. It wants to open its 200th shop early in 2027.
Tesco has about 13,700 workers. Their average pay is now €18.13 an hour.
Tesco Ireland also has a new boss. His name is Andrew Yaxley. He did the same job before, from 2015 to 2018. Food sales did very well this year.
Tesco's Irish business made 8.6% more profit before tax in its last financial year, which ended in February. Profit rose to €211.6 million, and sales grew from €3.45 billion to €3.75 billion.

The company paid €120 million to its British parent company, the same amount as the year before. It paid almost €32 million in corporation tax. For the first time, its saved-up profits are now over €1 billion.

Sales in existing shops grew by 4.6%, and food sales were especially strong. Tesco opened nine new shops and says its online service now reaches 92% of people in Ireland. It says its main aim is to make sure customers do not go elsewhere because of price, and it matched some prices with Aldi.

Tesco has 194 shops in Ireland and expects to open its 200th early in 2027. It employs 13,676 people, and the average hourly wage rose to €18.13. Andrew Yaxley has come back as head of Tesco Ireland, a job he first did from 2015 to 2018.
Tesco Ireland's pretax profit rose by 8.6% to €211.6 million in the financial year to the end of February, as turnover climbed to €3.75 billion from €3.45 billion.

The grocer paid a €120 million dividend to its British parent, unchanged from the previous year, and its corporation tax bill increased to almost €32 million. Its accumulated profits passed €1 billion for the first time, and its pretax margin edged up to 5.7%.

Like-for-like sales grew by 4.6%, with food performing particularly well. The company opened nine stores, launched a rapid delivery service and says its online business now covers 92% of the population. It says its priority is to remove price as a reason for shoppers to go elsewhere, and it ran a price-match scheme against Aldi.

Tesco, which claims 24.1% of the Irish grocery market, operates 194 stores in the Republic and expects to open its 200th early in 2027. Its workforce grew to 13,676, and the average hourly rate rose to €18.13. Andrew Yaxley has returned as chief executive, a role he previously held from 2015 to 2018.
